script: How do you currently stay informed about air quality in your neighborhood, and what sources do you rely on most?
Can you describe a recent experience where poor air quality affected your daily life or plans, and how did you cope with it?

If you were to pay €X per month for a personal air-quality sensor that would alert you via SMS when the air quality in your neighborhood exceeds a certain threshold, would you consider purchasing one?
interview_answers:
I actually don't have a personal smartphone with internet access at home. My husband usually checks the local newspaper or the official website of our town hall to get information about air quality. He's quite particular about it and likes to know if there are any smog alerts that might affect his work as a mechanic.

If I need to check the air quality myself, I usually go to the town square where they display the current pollution levels on an electronic screen. It's not very detailed, but at least it gives us an idea of how bad it is outside. Sometimes, the local TV station will also broadcast information about air quality if there are any serious problems in our area.

I have to admit, I wish we had more accurate and regular monitoring systems here in Ravenna, especially since my department deals with the public's health on a daily basis. But these resources help us get an idea of what's going on outside.

I remember last autumn when the air quality was really bad due to some wildfires in the nearby hills. My husband was scheduled to work at the garage, but he had to cancel his shift because of the smog alert. He didn't want to risk getting sick or having any trouble breathing while working with cars.

As for me, I actually had a meeting that day at the town hall where we discuss plans for the upcoming summer festival. The air quality was so bad that our department decided to postpone the outdoor activities and move everything indoors instead. It was a bit of an inconvenience, but we wanted to make sure everyone's health was prioritized.

To be honest, it was frustrating because some of the other departments were not as concerned about the air quality as my own department is. But I guess that's just part of our job - making sure everything runs smoothly and safely for the community.

We didn't have any of those new-fangled air-quality monitoring devices in our town square, so we relied on the traditional methods like checking the newspaper and watching TV to get updates. It was a bit old-fashioned, but it got the job done!

I'm not sure if I'd be willing to spend money on something like that. To be honest, the current information we get from the town hall and the electronic screen in the town square is already helping us stay informed about air quality.

If it were within my budget, which is quite limited, I would have to think carefully before committing to a personal air-quality sensor. €X per month might seem like a reasonable price, but for me, it's not something that's high on my list of priorities right now.
